short: Asia's first modern constitution, granted by the emperor and making him sacred and inviolable.
full:
Itō Hirobumi spent eighteen months in Europe from 1882 studying constitutional systems and came back convinced by the Prussian model rather than the British. The document he and Inoue Kowashi drafted, with advice from the German jurist Hermann Roesler, was promulgated on 11 February 1889 as a gift from the throne to the people — not a compact between them. It ran to seventy-six articles. The emperor was declared sacred and inviolable, head of state, and holder of the supreme command of the army and navy.

The Imperial Diet that first met in 1890 was genuinely elected, though the tax qualification limited the franchise to about one per cent of the population, and it could refuse a budget. But the service chiefs' right of direct access to the throne, outside the cabinet, gave the army a lever no civilian government could remove, and it was used repeatedly in the 1930s. The constitution was never amended in its fifty-eight years. It ceased to have effect when the post-war constitution came into force on 3 May 1947.
